16.0.0.en: Horn: from the horns of sheep, and it was used as a vessel for the anointing oil.

16.0.1.en: Bethlehem: located about 9.5 km south of Jerusalem.

16.0.2.en: God spoke to Samuel, asking him to stop weeping and making petition for Saul after He had rejected him as a result of his disobedience and contempt for His commands, and He commanded him to take a horn and put in it “the holy oil” and go with it to “Jesse,” who lives in the city of Bethlehem, to anoint one of his sons as king.

16.0.3.en: And God says, “I have provided Me ... a king”: God in His fatherhood chooses a king submissive to Him, to carry out His commandments and lead His people in the way of righteousness.

16.1.0.en: Samuel, in his human weakness, was afraid of Saul, the present king, lest he kill him if he learned that Samuel would anoint another king, and he said this to God. But God, in His long-suffering, did not rebuke Samuel for his human weakness, but gave him a solution, which was to take a heifer and go with it to Bethlehem as though he had gone to offer a sacrifice, which was acceptable and well known of Samuel, who traveled much in the land and offered sacrifices in every place. This was an exception that Samuel made, because the sacrifices were all offered in the house of God. Samuel’s saying that he would offer a sacrifice is not a lie, because he would indeed offer it before all the people, but he would anoint the new king secretly.

16.1.1.en: The secret anointing of David is a symbol of our present life, for we have all been anointed with the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Holy Myron, but our kingship and coronation will be revealed in eternity (Rom 8:18) after our death, which is symbolized by the death of Saul, and after we pass through the sufferings of this present time, which are symbolized by the sufferings David endured from Saul.

16.2.0.en: God continues His speech with Samuel and says to him, “Invite Jesse and his house to attend the sacrifice, and you shall anoint the son whom I shall declare to you, and I will tell you all that you shall do.”

16.3.0.en: Samuel carried out God’s word and came to Bethlehem, and when the elders of the city saw him they were afraid because his visit was sudden, and they thought that he had come to announce an error or punish someone, so they asked him, “Do you come in goodness and peace, or for another purpose?”

16.4.0.en: Samuel reassured them and said to them ... “I have only come to offer a sacrifice to the Lord, and there is no bad news in my coming,” and he asked them to sanctify themselves before the offering of the sacrifice, and likewise he asked “Jesse” and his sons, and invited everyone to the sacrifice. The sanctification was done by a person bathing, washing his clothes and examining his conscience ...

16.4.1.en: The priest cries out in the Liturgy, saying, “The holies are for the holy,” before the people come forward to partake of the Holy Mysteries. Examine yourself, beloved, and sanctify yourself by repentance and purifying your conscience, and you will receive the blessing of union with the Body and Blood of Christ.

16.5.0.en: When they had come: Samuel, Jesse and his sons went to the house of Jesse, and this was at Samuel’s command, so that he might secretly accomplish the anointing of the new king.

16.5.1.en: Samuel offered the sacrifice on an altar in the midst of the city but went to eat of it in the house of Jesse, of course with a prior purpose in his mind, and while he was in the house of Jesse, Samuel saw Jesse’s firstborn son “Eliab” and said in himself, “This is the Lord’s anointed.”

16.6.0.en: God made clear to Samuel that Eliab was not the new king as Samuel had thought because of his tall stature, and He declared to him that man looks at the outward appearance of the king, but God chooses the pure heart, so that the king may govern His people with godliness and righteousness.

16.7.0.en: In these three verses Jesse presented his seven sons before Samuel, beginning with “Abinadab,” his second son, then “Shammah,” his third son, to the last of the seven, but with each of them God declared to Samuel that he was not the one chosen to be anointed king.

16.8.0.en: Since the Lord did not choose any of these seven, Samuel asked “Jesse,” “Are these all your children?” and “Jesse” answered him that there remained only the youngest, who was charged with keeping the sheep. Samuel asked “Jesse” to bring him, and quickly, expressing his concern for the coming of this young one by saying that he would not sit down to eat until he arrived.

16.9.0.en: Indeed Jesse sent and summoned his youngest son “David,” and he came, and Samuel describes him as beautiful in appearance and form, his complexion tending to whiteness, and his eyes also colored. And when the youth David came in, the Lord declared to Samuel that he was the chosen one and asked him to arise and anoint him.

16.9.1.en: We see here that David, the youngest, left with the sheep, whom no one expected to be the one chosen by God, is indeed chosen by God because of his faithfulness in tending the sheep, for he killed the lion and the bear and risked himself to keep the sheep (ch. 17:34). David represents all those despised and rejected by the world whose hearts are pure and faithful, for they are advanced before God. He also symbolizes the Gentiles, who were rejected by the Jews, but Christ, who came for the salvation of all, accepted them, and many saints came out of them. David here also symbolizes Christ, despised, born in the manger, persecuted by the priests, scribes and Pharisees, and crucified, yet He is the Savior of the whole world and the King of kings. It also appears from this that God’s view differs from people’s view, so He chose David, whom even his father did not feel to be suitable for this office. So do not judge by appearance, and give room for prayer to hear God’s voice and His choice.

16.10.0.en: Indeed Samuel arose and anointed “David” with the holy oil before all who were present, and immediately the Spirit of God came upon David as the anointed of the Lord and king of Israel all his days. As for Samuel, after he had completed his mission, he set out returning to Ramah, his place of residence, after he had anointed David and eaten of the sacrifice.

16.10.1.en: David believed in the grace of God that had come upon him to be king, but when he did not find himself declared crowned over the kingdom, but Saul who was reigning, perhaps he understood that he needed a period of preparation for the kingship, in which God would prepare him, so he was not troubled and lived his normal life and did not demand any rights of kingship. Perhaps this preparation appears in:

16.10.2.en: 1- His learning to shepherd the people through his shepherding of the sheep.

16.10.3.en: 2- His learning meditation and solitude with God, who would support him in his life and in his office as king.

16.10.4.en: 3- His learning to play the lute to praise God and thank Him for everything, so that he would not be troubled by the sufferings that might pass over him.

16.10.5.en: 4- In his victory over the lion and the bear he felt the power of God supporting him.

16.10.6.en: 5- His playing the lute for Saul let him see the royal palace and learn how the king conducts the affairs of the kingdom.

16.10.7.en: 6- In his victory over Goliath and killing him, his faith in the power of God who was with him was confirmed.

16.10.8.en: 7- Saul’s jealousy of him taught him to make excuses for others, to have pity on them and to love them.

16.10.9.en: 8- His endurance of sufferings and exile when Saul pursued him made him not attached to the delights and luxury of the kingship, and he remained holding fast to his love for God.

16.10.10.en: 9- His exposure to being killed by Saul many times made him rely on God and trust in His protection of him.

16.10.11.en: 10- Saul’s falling into his hands during the pursuit taught him complete forgiveness and respect for others.

16.10.12.en: Do not judge by appearance, lest your judgment be wrong. Seek God and be deliberate in judgment if you are responsible for choosing a person to bear a certain responsibility, and be long-suffering until God reveals to you the suitable person. And do not interfere in what does not concern you and judge others, so that you fall into condemnation.

16.11.s.en: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

16.11.0.en: After Saul had erred more than once and despised God’s commands, and the Lord had declared his rejection, the Holy Spirit left him completely, and by God’s permission an unclean spirit suddenly came upon him and he became a dwelling of Satan, and this spirit kept troubling Saul and tormenting him from time to time.

16.11.1.en: This does not mean that God sent him an unclean spirit, but because of his evil God forsook him, so the unclean spirit entered him, and God allowed this to show the result of pride and evil.

16.12.0.en: With the repeated attacks of the evil spirit on Saul, his servants suggested to him that he send his men everywhere in the kingdom to search for a man skilled in playing the strings, so that if such a man were found and played his melodies while the unclean spirit was active and tormenting Saul, the spirit would be calmed and Saul would be at rest and his soul would be well. Perhaps this suggestion was considered a kind of treatment of agitation by calm music, which often succeeds ... But he did not know that all this was a prior divine arrangement so that Saul would meet David the son of Jesse. And no one dared to confront the king and call him to repentance so that the unclean spirit would leave him.

16.13.0.en: Indeed Saul commanded his men and servants to search for a man skilled in playing, and one of Saul’s acquaintances who was present said that he knew a man whom he had seen, one of the sons of “Jesse” of Bethlehem, and this son was not only a good player of music but also a bold man and a warrior, with the speech of the wise, and handsome in appearance, and above all this the Lord was with him and blessed him.

16.14.0.en: When Saul heard this testimony he did not search for anyone else but sent messengers to Bethlehem asking “Jesse” to send his son who kept the sheep. Indeed “Jesse” sent his son David to the king and sent with him a gift consisting of bread, wine and a kid of the goats, for he was a generous and distinguished man and thought it good to send his son with a gift for the king.

16.15.0.en: David came in to King Saul in his council, and the Lord gave him favor in the king’s eyes, so he loved him greatly from the time he saw him and made him one of his close men, making him his armor-bearer, which means that he was constantly beside Saul. And Saul sent a messenger to “Jesse,” David’s father, asking him to leave David to him because he loved him and trusted him and made him one of the nearest men of the people to him. Of course Jesse could not refuse such a request, but considered this an honor for any father in all Israel.

16.15.1.en: David’s presence in the royal palace was an opportunity for him to become acquainted with the system of government and its management, to learn everything useful for ruling and avoid the errors that harm the people, so that this would be a preparation and groundwork for him when he actually takes the leadership of the people.

16.16.0.en: Whenever the unclean spirit attacked Saul, David would play the strings of his lute, and the unclean spirit would depart from the king and he would be refreshed afterward. The reason for the removal of the unclean spirit was not merely the playing of music, but the basis was the presence of David the righteous, so that Satan feared him and departed from Saul.

16.16.1.en: If you are faithful in your work and in bearing responsibility, God gives you favor in the eyes of those in authority, and even gives you dignity as well, which you can use to draw them to God.

17.0.s.en: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

17.0.0.en: Socoh: 14 miles southwest of Jerusalem, beside the southern border of the tribe of Judah, that is, near the Philistines.

17.0.2.en: Ephes-dammim: located northeast of Socoh at a distance of four miles.

17.0.3.en: The Philistines gathered for war against Israel and made for themselves a camp in which they drew up their ranks between three places, which are Socoh, Azekah and Ephes-dammim.

17.1.0.en: The valley of the terebinth: the valley of acacia trees.

17.1.1.en: As for Israel, they gathered under the leadership of Saul in a valley in which acacia trees abound and drew up in ranks for war opposite the army of the Philistines.

17.2.0.en: Both sides stood on a hill, and each army could see the other completely and even hear it, and a valley separated the two sides. Each of the two parties feared to go down into the valley lest the other strike it, and when the time grew long, Goliath took this opportunity to come forward and ask for a champion to fight him, as will appear in what follows.

17.3.0.en: Champion: one who fights with his sword face to face with another champion.

17.3.1.en: A man from the ranks of the Philistines, whose name was Goliath, came forward. He was from one of the five great cities of the Philistines, which is the city of Gath, and his height by present-day measures was more than three meters, and of course his breadth was proportionate to his height, since he was a man of war.

17.4.0.en: Scale armor: on the armor there are scales of bronze like the scales of a fish.

17.4.1.en: This man was dreadful in his clothing, war equipment and weapons. He covered his head with a helmet of bronze and wore armor protecting his chest, also of bronze, and the surface of this armor was covered with bronze rings resembling fish scales. This armor was massive, for its weight reached 55 kilograms, considering that the weight of the shekel ranges from

17.5.0.en: Greaves: thin sheets of bronze wrapped around the leg to protect the fighter.

17.5.1.en: Javelin: a small spear, shorter in length than the spear and longer and thicker than the arrow.

17.5.2.en: Goliath wore on his legs something like a bronze stocking to protect his legs, and carried on his back between the shoulders a small bronze javelin.

17.6.0.en: The spear: it is the lance, and its shaft was of wood and its head of pointed iron.

17.6.1.en: Goliath also carried a huge spear with a large, broad wooden shaft resembling the beam of the loom used in weaving, which is a broad, heavy piece of wood. His spear did not have a single iron point like the other spears but a group of points like a fork, and the weight of the points of his spear was about seven kilograms of iron ... He had a shield, which is usually round and which the fighter holds with his left arm to ward off attacks, and in the case of Goliath a man was assigned to carry the shield for him until there was fighting, and then Goliath would carry it himself, and perhaps the reason for having a man carry the shield for him was the weight of his clothing and war equipment. And of course, dear reader, if we review what was written in the description of Goliath, we know that we are before a huge human tank, for in all the history of mankind there has been no one whose height reached three meters.

17.7.0.en: Goliath came forward and called in a loud voice to the drawn-up army of Israel, saying to them, “Why do you fight with all your men? For I am here representing all the Philistines and you are all Saul’s men. So why do you not choose from among you a man to fight me face to face instead of shedding the blood of men in war? If this man is able to defeat me, all the Philistines will become servants to you, but if I defeat him and kill him, all of you with your people will become servants to us, the Philistines.” He said this confident that there would be no one who dared to stand before him.

17.8.1.en: With the arrogance of one confident of victory, Goliath continued his speech, saying, “I have challenged all the Philistines and have not found a single man among them to come out to meet me and fight me.”

17.9.0.en: The offer that Goliath made was a new offer, not customary among peoples in wars, and his huge and awesome appearance with all that he wore was terrifying to whoever saw him. For this reason all Saul’s men were afraid and kept silent, and of course not a single man of them came forward.

17.9.1.en: Do not fear Satan, who uses the wicked to threaten and terrify you, for they are worthless before God however strong they appear. Seek God’s help and trust that He is able to rescue you from their hands, and fight for you and glorify you.

17.10.s.en: (2) Jesse sends David to visit his brothers

17.10.0.en: This verse takes us back to the family of Jesse, who was from Ephrath, “Bethlehem,” of the tribe of Judah, and he had eight sons, the youngest of whom was “David,” whom Samuel anointed as king; he also had three sons in the war, who were the eldest, “Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah.” The man wanted to be reassured about his sons, but he had grown old and aged and was not able to go himself to check on them.

17.11.0.en: David had been staying with Saul as his armor-bearer (ch. 16), but when the battle began, and because he was too young to be counted among the men of war, he went to his father’s house to tend the sheep, though from time to time he would go to Saul to play the lute for him when the unclean spirit attacked him.

17.12.0.en: As for the field of battle, there was no fighting there, but Goliath kept coming out and advancing and taunting and challenging all the people and the men of war for forty days, coming out twice every day, morning and evening, and of course no one dared to meet him.

17.13.0.en: Ephah: a measure holding about 22.9 liters, and equal to about 10 kg of parched grain (freekeh).

17.13.1.en: Token: a sign or anything that confirms that he met his brothers, because writing was not widespread in those days.

17.13.2.en: The father Jesse charged his youngest son David with the mission of going to the place of battle to check on his brothers and supply them with food, represented by the parched grain as well as ready-to-eat bread, and the generous man did not forget to present to the captain of the thousand, who was the commander over his brothers, ten cheeses as a gift. And “Jesse” asked David to bring back on his return tokens from his brothers by which he could be sure of their well-being and that they were still alive.

17.14.0.en: Saul was still in the valley of the terebinth with his men, facing the army of the Philistines, but without any real fighting worth mentioning. The expression “fighting with the Philistines” means that they were in a state of readiness for war.

17.14.1.en: How beautiful it is that you take care to ask about your loved ones and to visit those who are absent from the Church, to check on them and encourage them to attend, for a question of love has a great effect on hearts.

17.15.s.en: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

17.15.0.en: The barricade: the barricades are the obstacles that the drawn-up army sets before it to hinder the enemy, and they may be of logs cut from trees, or earthen barriers, or stones.

17.15.1.en: David left the sheep with a hired keeper and set out early, carrying the bread, the parched grain and the cheeses, as his father had commanded him, and this shows his distinction in obedience, for it was swift, and this qualifies him for his office as king in his obedience to God. When he reached the area of the barricades, the men were drawn up in ranks, singing the stirring songs and shouts of war.

17.16.0.en: Both armies stood facing each other, but David left all that he had brought with a man of the army who was assigned to keep deposits, called the keeper of the baggage, to give it to the soldiers at a later time, and went quickly to check on his brothers.

17.17.0.en: David reached the front lines and met his brothers, and brotherly conversation went on between them, and while he was there Goliath came out to repeat what he said every day of taunting the people of God, and none of the people answered him. David of course heard him, and also noticed the fear of all the men and their drawing back.

17.18.0.en: In the face of the people’s great fear, Saul promised a reward to whoever would confront Goliath. First, the king would enrich him with a large monetary reward that would make him one of the great men of the kingdom; the second gift was that this man would be given his daughter in marriage, so that the king himself would become his relative; and the third reward was that his father’s house would be exempted from taxes and from the service of the king and from any other forced labor. Yet no man came forward to fight Goliath.

17.19.0.en: Uncircumcised: that is, he was not circumcised (purified) like the rest of the males of the people of Israel.

17.19.1.en: David addressed the men around him, saying, “What shall be done for the man who kills Goliath and takes away the reproach from the people of Israel?” and he asked in a tone of disapproval, “Who is this pagan, uncircumcised Philistine that he should insult and taunt the people of the living God by his words?...!” David’s question was based on zeal and enthusiasm for his people and for the name of God.

17.20.0.en: The men answered David with the three rewards of the king which he had promised in (v. 25).

17.21.0.en: Eliab heard David’s words with the men, so he became angry with him and rebuked him, saying, “Why have you come down to the field of battle, and why have you left your work of keeping the sheep?” and he accused him of the pride that drove him to learn the news of the war in order to boast of it among his young companions. Of course Eliab was wrong in all that he said, and accused his brother in it of curiosity and of seeking to raise his own standing.

17.22.0.en: As for David, with wisdom he absorbed his brother’s anger, saying, “What have I now done?” or is it just talk, conversation, and question and answer? And with intelligence also he removed from himself the suspicion that he was thinking of fighting Goliath, so that his brother might be reassured.

17.23.0.en: No sooner had David turned his back, moving away from his eldest brother, than he kept asking here and there and repeating his saying about how “this uncircumcised one taunts the people of the living God,” and the words were passed from man to man until the men told Saul of David’s bold words, full of confidence, so Saul sent and brought David before him. From this appear some virtues that qualified David to prevail over the mighty Goliath:

17.23.1.en: 1- Obedience: which appeared in his swift obedience to his father (v. 20).

17.23.2.en: 2- Wisdom: in his answer to his eldest brother “Eliab” and his not being disturbed by his rebuke (v. 28).

17.23.3.en: 3- His zeal for the name of God, for he did not fight Goliath to prove his strength because he was his personal enemy, but because of his daring to insult the name of God (v. 10), unlike Saul, who considered the Philistines his enemies and not the enemies of God (ch. 14:24).

17.23.4.en: 4- Self-giving: he was ready to give his life to redeem his people when he agreed to fight Goliath, and his asking about the king’s reward for whoever defeats Goliath was an understanding of everything surrounding the matter of Goliath and not an attachment to a reward, because nothing is dearer than a person’s life, and if he dies no reward will benefit him (v. 27).

17.24.0.en: When David met Saul, he spoke to him first, reassuring the king and trusting in God who supports him, and told him that there was no need for anyone to fear this uncircumcised one or feel humiliated, for he was fully ready to go and kill this Philistine.

17.25.0.en: Despite the king’s great need of any volunteer to go and fight Goliath so as to remove the shame from his people, his love for David and his pity for him on the one hand, and his realistic view of the matter on the other, made him advise David to give up the matter, pointing out to him his young age and that Goliath was a man experienced in war all his life. For Saul thought that David’s words were merely youthful impulsiveness on his part.

17.26.0.en: David’s enthusiasm did not wane in the face of Saul’s words, and in an attempt to convince him that he was not the tender lad but had the heart of a fighting man, he began to tell Saul a story that had happened to him: that one day, while he was tending his father’s sheep, a mountain lion and also a bear came out against him, and the lion was able to snatch a young sheep in its mouth. Of course in such circumstances the shepherd thanks God that the lion did not come near him personally and that the loss is considered a slight loss since it was a single sheep, but the shepherd with the fiery heart did not do this; rather he took his staff and chased the lion desperately and struck it and knocked it down and rescued the sheep from its mouth, and when the lion rose again from its faint, David seized it again by its beard and kept striking its head until he killed it, and he killed the bear also.

17.27.0.en: David continued his speech: “Your servant has killed a lion and a bear, which are among the most ferocious of animals, so likewise will be the fate of Goliath the uncircumcised Philistine, who has permitted himself to taunt the people of the living God, and God Himself, who delivered me from the lion and the bear, will give me victory over Goliath and rescue me from death.” In the face of this courage and faith of David, Saul could do nothing but agree, and he prayed for God’s blessing on his steps.

17.28.0.en: As a kind of appreciation and reward, Saul rose and took off his war clothes and put them on David, and also gave him a bronze helmet and armor, and after that David took Saul’s sword as well and tried to move. It was the first time in his life that he moved in war clothing, and he found them very heavy and hindering him from moving, and he told Saul that he could not walk, so he put the clothes off him, that is, took them off.

17.28.1.en: Here a question appears: where is the brave Jonathan, who had earlier attacked the Philistines alone with his armor-bearer (ch. 14)? Why did he not come forward to Goliath?! This shows how difficult it was to confront this huge monster of a warrior, so Jonathan feared him.

17.28.2.en: And David here is a symbol of Christ, whom no one else could overcome Satan and bind him by the Cross.

17.28.3.en: Be humble if someone rebukes you even if he is not right, for your long-suffering and love absorb the anger of others, so you win them and keep your peace.

17.29.1.en: Shepherd’s bag: a sack or pouch in which the shepherd carries his food and carries it on his shoulder.

17.29.2.en: Sling: a strip of cloth in the middle of which stones are placed in preparation for hurling them.

17.29.3.en: After David took off the heavy war clothes and became light in movement, he took the staff that shepherds carry and chose five stones (pebbles) from the ground of the valley and put them in the shepherd’s bag hung on his shoulder, and took his sling in his other hand and advanced in the low valley between the two armies toward the huge Goliath.

17.30.0.en: Goliath also advanced toward David, and when he found him without war clothing and its equipment, and also young, slight of body and delicate of features, he despised him in himself and mocked him, and regarded David’s coming out to meet him as unworthy of his position and strength, so he began to curse David and revile the God of Israel, and said to David in his mockery, “Do you think I am a dog and not a warrior, that you come out against me with a staff instead of a sword or a spear?”

17.31.0.en: In anger Goliath threatened David to terrify him and said, “Come and advance toward me, and I will make you a tasty meal for the birds of prey of the sky and the beasts of the earth.”

17.32.0.en: David said to Goliath his famous and well-remembered word, declaring in it his strong faith in the God of Israel and in the power of His holy name, which is: if you come to me relying on your weapons, sword, spear and shield, I take refuge in the name of the God of the heavenly hosts and the God of Israel, whom you have despised and whose people you have taunted insolently.

17.33.0.en: Then David said, “Now God will deliver you into my hand, and by His power I will kill you and cut off your head; indeed God will give me victory over all your people, so that all your people will become food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, and your people first, and all the peoples of the earth second, will know that the God of Israel is a God able to do all things and that no command is too hard for Him. And it will be a lesson to all who are watching, present at this encounter, that victory is not by human weapons and the instruments of war, but God alone is the One who delivers you into our hands despite your apparent strength and your many numbers.”

17.34.0.en: It sank: it was embedded in his forehead.

17.34.1.en: When Goliath advanced in his steps toward David, David also quickly advanced toward him and put in his sling a stone from the five stones and stretched out his arm to hurl the stone, and indeed the stone flew through the air on its way to Goliath’s forehead and sank into it. The shock of the stone was so violent that it made this mighty man lose his balance, and he fell on his face to the ground. And so David prevailed over Goliath without a sword, and threw him to the ground and killed him.

17.34.2.en: From this it appears that however strong a person is, he has a point of weakness, even if only one, and Goliath’s point of weakness was that his forehead was not protected, so David was able to hunt him with a small pebble by the dog sling which he used to drive dogs away from his sheep. So do not be disturbed by the strength of enemies, because God is able to overcome them easily.

17.35.0.en: Drew it out of its sheath: brought it out of its scabbard.

17.35.1.en: This verse gives the detail of the summary that came in (v. 50). After Goliath fell to the ground, David ran quickly to him as he lay on his face and drew Goliath’s sword from its scabbard, raised it with both hands and brought it down on his neck, cutting off his head and killing him, and before the terror and severity of the surprise the Philistines trembled and fled.

17.36.0.en: Shaaraim: one of the cities of Judah in the valley of acacias.

17.36.1.en: All the people rose after the Philistines who fled to their cities “Gath and Ekron” and killed many of them and pursued them to the valley near their cities.

17.36.2.en: It is noted that the tribe of Judah is mentioned by name separately from the rest of the tribes, in honor of the tribe from which came the victorious David and the coming king of all the people.

17.37.0.en: Taking shelter: in other translations, “the pursuit.”

17.37.1.en: After the people had finished pursuing the Philistines, they returned quickly to the place where the Philistines had been encamped and took possession of all the spoil or goods that they had left behind.

17.38.0.en: As for David, he took care to carry and take the head of Goliath, who had been killed, and brought it to Jerusalem, and likewise he kept Goliath’s sword and the rest of his weapons in his tent in preparation for moving them to the house of the Lord as a memorial of God’s work with His people and His great victory (ch. 21).

17.38.1.en: David was not disturbed by the hugeness and strength of Goliath or by his weapons, but in faith he advanced toward him and by the power of God was able to kill him. So believe in God, who protects you and works through you, and you will advance to the hardest circumstances confident of your success by His power, and even if many oppose you, they cannot hinder you or overcome the God who is in you.

17.39.0.en: This verse takes us back to before David’s encounter with Goliath and his killing him. After David’s dialogue with Saul to convince him of his going to the war, and David’s actually going out, Saul asked Abner, the commander of his army, about David, saying, “Whose son is this lad?”

17.39.1.en: This arouses wonder, for Saul had earlier loved David and made him his armor-bearer, so how does he ask about him now? To answer this question we explain the following:

17.39.2.en: 1- David did not have a permanent residence in Saul’s house, but they would summon him whenever Saul was troubled, and in the last period the unclean spirit had not been attacking Saul, and consequently David’s appearances with him were not frequent.

17.39.3.en: 2- The title of the king’s armor-bearer was more an honorary title for one whom the king wished to honor, and perhaps David carried Saul’s weapons for some days and then left this task to take care of the sheep of his father “Jesse.” Perhaps years passed between David’s playing the lute before Saul and his killing Goliath, in addition to the fact that the unclean spirit made Saul forget many things.

17.39.4.en: There is another opinion, which is that Saul was jealous of David and showed that he did not know him, out of neglect of him, and Abner followed him in that.

17.40.0.en: Saul charged “Abner,” the commander of his army, to inquire about David and his lineage, and indeed when David had finished killing Goliath, “Abner” brought him before Saul while he was still carrying Goliath’s head in his hand, and Saul asked him, “Whose son are you, lad, and of whom of the people?” and David answered him that he was the son of “Jesse” of the village of Bethlehem. In David’s answer his humility before the king is noted, for he said, “the son of your servant.”

17.40.1.en: David, by his victory over Goliath, is a symbol of Christ in the following:

17.40.2.en: 1- David killed the mighty man who taunted the people of God, and Christ bound Satan, who fights and taunts the children of God.

17.40.3.en: 2- David cut off Goliath’s head, and Christ by His death trampled the head of the ancient serpent, that is, Satan.

17.40.4.en: 3- David killed Goliath with Goliath’s sword, and Christ trampled Satan by the Cross and His death upon it, which Satan arranged through the high priests of the Jews.

17.40.5.en: 4- David took a staff in his hand when he met Goliath, and Christ carried the wood of the Cross.

17.40.6.en: Be humble when you achieve victories, accomplishments and successes, giving the glory to God with thanksgiving, and you will protect yourself from pride and receive more abundant divine blessings.

17.40.7.en: Jonathan’s friendship and Saul’s enmity toward David
